blocks.x: All right, let me put on where we're recording it. Recording it at this tape at 925 Moray Street, that's right. 925 Moray Street is right. Mm-hmm. And what's today's date? October?
So you were talking about how the collection went. Yes.

Yes, the thing goes around with the little basket for that beat and the choir would be singing and everything going on with anybody. When the friends put in there they cater up to the table and they dump it over there and they account the money. Then when the church is over they tell you what they speak up.
And who does that money go to?
To the church.
To the church. Yeah.
Not no one person. If it's for the up building of the church, they keep the church in good condition.
Well does the preacher get paid out of that?
No, the preacher gets salary, a month. He gets so much money. But that money they pick up like that, he don't taste that. His hands don't taste that at all. He has a committee.
Now is there any other way that they collect the money other than passing the plates?

Well, sometimes they have an envelope sometimes. They give every member of the church, you understand? Well, they have a dish set for everybody to come and bring in the envelope. See? That's for the church too. That's for the up building of the church.
Well, do you walk up front with the envelope or do you hand it to somebody or what?
No, you can sit right down there. They got someone to come and pick it up if you don't feel like you're anything. Do they ever walk up with the envelope?
They could walk up with it.
Yeah, and give it. Yeah, sure. But I mean, in the event, you don't feel like getting up here. You can put it in a basket and put it on the table, you see?

Well, I have seen people walk around, like the members of the club walk around in the church and they all line up and come up front and walk around and around several times. And they usually drop off quarters.

Well, you can walk around, you can walk around because every time you walk around there, then in that table you got to put something on that table. If you're going to keep walking around there, every time you get to that spot there, you got to put on something. And sometimes they have a dollar match, sometimes a five dollar match. You know what I'm saying? You make it around, you put it on the table.
So you have to start out with plenty in your pocket.
Yeah, but of course you can put what you want, you understand?
Well, what is a dollar match exactly?

Well, I'm going to tell you that that's some of the guys just, you understand, want to put on a big seat. Well, are we going to have a dollar match? Well, that goes for the ushers or the second board or something like that, you understand? They want to be big, you understand? And they say, the dollar match, what? And the dollar match, are you all going to do any good? You put that dollar on the table. That's a pretty good way too. If you feel like, if you feel like they want one, they want to be a B-shot, they'll even be a B-shot. And go and put it on the table.
There's something else I was wondering about now. Say, do you ever hear of brass bands giving a sample to anybody? Say the Widow or somebody or the club? Give them what? A sample of the music. No.
You mean before they hired?
Before they hired, yeah. To give them an idea how they sound.
No. No, since I've been playing.
So they find out about the brass bands another way then?

Well, yeah, but I'm going to tell you, in a way, they knows all the brass bands. Oh, since. They got all the society and things around there. They got men in there who know every band in the age around there, you see. They have some men in society that used to be an old musician, you understand? So they know, you see. You can't fool them a bit. They know the best and the worst, they know the worst.
And even if they weren't, they probably grew up as second liners. I mean, they've heard them all their lives, I guess.
Yeah, I see. They've heard them all their lives. That's right.
I'd like to talk to some of those guys from the society who helped to choose the band, you know, and stuff. If you can get any of them's names or addresses.

But I tell you, the best way you can get there, you see Ray or Paiso or the other person where you see them, they keep all that. But we all, we don't worry about that. We just worry about the guy's job. If you call the upteller, you meet, see the person even going on. But otherwise, we don't worry about it, see.
Well, let's see. Back to what goes on in the church. You got offerings, singing, and the preachers get up and preach.
Yeah, yeah.
And then what else happens?

They preach and then when they finish everything, they finish the day, the collection and everything, and then the preacher get up and then he announce what's going to happen in the next five or the next five years. or six days, you see. And then they napt after that. The benediction. No. Then he out.
He's talking about a regular Sunday church service now.
No, I mean at a funeral.
They announce what's going to happen in the next five or six days at a funeral?
Oh, no. You said about the church, you see.
Yeah, well I meant at the church at a funeral.

Oh, no, no. They don't do that. Yeah. You're living at the funeral, no. When they finish preaching at church, all they're doing in the picture, when they finish, they dismiss the church and then they bring the body on that.
But I thought maybe some members of the congregation would speak or they'd come up and view the body or something.

Oh, well, before they leave the church, you see, when they fixin' to leave the church, they tell you, come around and view the body. And then you come around and view the body, and as you view the body, you come on up. You see? Wow. And then after you view the body, then on the church, close the body and then you catch it up. And then they come on up.
Do they open up the whole lid or do they have a half a lid or what on those colors?
They got a half lid there. You can see the face and everything. We're down there. Time to around the stomach.
Yeah, sure. Yeah, that's the way it's been when I've seen them.
I just read it now.
Do they have flowers with the body in the church or not?
Yeah, you do have flowers in the church.
Any other kind of decoration or anything with the body?
No, no more than flowers and bouquet of flowers and a wreath, what I'll say, you can see, designed.
Well, now, how would the body be dressed?
Well, that's up to the family, you see. They choose what kind of garment that they want to put on the folks, you see. It's up to them. And they can put anything you want on.
Well, what do they usually have, though?
Well, if you're a man, if you have your own suit, if you want them to put that on, you're sorry. But if you want to get a suit from the undertaker, well, they put that on you. See?
Would it be a regular suit or a tuxedo or what?
Well, you just, any kind of stuff you want, you just depend on that.
I see. Now, suppose he's a member of an organization. Would he have any of that uniform on?
Well, no. If they want to, they can put it on. But it's up to the family, you understand, what they want to put on. There's the bosses leaving.
I see.
Well, do the Masons ever hire a band of music for their funerals?
Sometimes. Yes.
Because they always seem to have pretty much ceremony in themselves. I mean, you know.
Yes, yes. They are.
Let's see. What happens after you come out of the church now?
What happens after you come into the church?
With the body.
Oh, well. This is that. Beforehand, you place the fumes, the dodges. But now, I guess, this is what you want to find out. After you leave the cemetery, you know? Is that what you mean?
Well, no. I mean, what happens? You go from the church to the cemetery. Absolutely. And then what happens when you get in the cemetery?

In the cemetery, you place a hand, you know, or a few of them. A few of them, a few of them, a kind of a short, you understand? And then after the pretty minute tour, or after you beat them somewhere there, when you finish. You know, you know, you're a place where you're a little piece of open, you understand? You go out of the people, you know, to tell me again or else now, the upper garden sets up my church, you understand? And then that's it. That's all. So they bury them and then you come outside? Yeah, you come outside and wait for the society. And then when they come up, all they say, let's go.
And then what happens?
Anything, a lot happens.
Where do you all head back for then? I mean, just follow wherever the Grand North shall lead here or what?

Yeah, yeah, far away. But here mostly have a route to go, you understand, all the time. He got to figure out if he kind of get out around the way to the block, if he had to go this way, he got to make a route there. So his gal would see him, you understand? And then he'd go on to the hall.
Where'd he end up? He got to go to the hall. So you end up where you started?
Absolutely, that's where I started.
And what kind of music?

You can play anything you want. Coming back. But we all, the way we're going to do it, when we leave the cemetery, we play on him, you understand? But then after we had him, he'd rip that, and then that cemetery, anything will happen.
Well, do they feed you and such when you get back to the hall?
Oh no, no, no. If you don't feed yourself, you ain't a devil ever fix it.
Let me ask you one more thing about the music. Sometimes I've heard where they just have a drum roll, it seems to me. Is that when they're moving the body sometimes? When just the drummer plays?

You see, when the drummer roll, when the drummer roll, and the drummer beats all the time, it's a different thing. You see, when they're drumming the roll, they're fixing to play it. But now when they're marching, they just beat the march on it. But when they go to roll, like that, well, they're fixing to play a piece.
The drummer will keep a beat going between the tunes. The roll serves as an introduction.
Yeah, sometimes it just seemed to me that they rolled the whole time when the body was, you know, being lifted out of the car or something.
I didn't know that was the sound. Yeah, well, that's what I'm telling me. When the body, that's what I'm telling me. You drum roll, roll, and then at that, the bass drum come in and hits.
The band comes in. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Bass drum gives you a little beat first. A roll, then a little bass drum beat, and then the band. Three beats. How many beats? Three beats? One, two, three.

Yeah. Or sometimes they, it's one, two, three. The whole time, in the bass drum, he hit the three, when the fellow's drum, he's supposed to hold and they roll until he finished. He beat them three, and three licks on the drum.
What are some of the tunes they play coming back, and what do they mean? I mean, do they play them for any special reason?
Oh, well, they're just anything that they, they're just anything they feel they're playing. They want to play the blues, they play, they're just anything they feel they're playing, they play.
What does the blues mean? I mean, what?
I don't know. They call me, they call me the blues, I just, and I just, I know, but.
I mean, is there any special reason for playing the blues?
No, no. Sometimes, some of the guys in the parade, they ask for them for anything, you see? And I propose, just what they ask for, why we play.
Would there be any reason why you play Lady Be Good?
Oh, well, that's a good one. I'll let it play that.
I know you have that on the record.
Yeah, I'll let it play that. It's very good. I love more than me, I play as a face.
How fast would you play coming back from the cemetery?
Well, you couldn't play too fast, playing in the march tempo.
Not the dirge tempo, but the regular march tempo.
Yeah, absolutely. A little faster than the dorge.
Let me see. How much does it pay?

Well, they pay, I believe, six to five dollars, six to five or seven dollars, seven dollars. I know when they went out, you know, they're going to give you six dollars on the man, except the leader, of course, you know, they get more.
The leader gets more, huh? What about the manager? Does he get more?
Well, he's here, I guess, them guys, they split it up, I guess.
What about when you first came here, how much were they paying for funerals then?
I mean, just two dollars, two and a half.
Well, how much of that money would you keep? I mean, by the time you got home?
Yeah, how much do I keep?
Yeah, well, I mean, you got to feed. All of it. All of it, and you'd go straight home?
I'd have it in there.
You mean, so you'd go straight home after you played a few hours? He said he'd have it in here.
I see. It's gone, and I guess the price of drinking's gone up in the years in between.

Well, let me tell you one thing. You see, I and Al, right now, but I mean, you know, when I was at the event, when we go on the film, we just go on there, just to be on there, just to have fun. You see, when we get home, we might have two dollars or three dollars out of the six, because we didn't drink the other part up.
Well, you strictly couldn't support yourself that way, could you?

Well, you see, we didn't depend on that for youngster and, no, not for youngster. Me, I read, I used to play them job. I just like to be in the street. I used to love the job, understand the bean and the street, you know, just play a few on the parade. But when I used to go play, we'd just go play there so we could drink, but for anything else, you know.
Well, in the old days, did any of the guys support themselves by playing in brass bands only?

Well, no, they couldn't exactly, just in brass bands only. Some of them used to play at night, but they didn't, they didn't play in the brass bands. Because myself, I used to play in the music box every night. That was on Cronlade and St. Charles, a jitney dance. And I used to play it every night, but in the film, sometimes we'd have a film every day, putting it. And I was like, well, you see, I just started. But of course, at that time when I was playing, I played in the middle of the way, I couldn't drink. Like I couldn't, I asked for that instant, but just nothing. Because I had to work at night, then work at night. You know, you couldn't, you couldn't make it that way. You just drinking and wasting all night. And I walked in the middle.
Well, it seems to me some of the people I know could play a funeral or parade and end up losing money, you know? I mean they could come out in the hole, huh? That would happen, huh?
Well, if you're going to suck it up, what do you expect? You got to lose.
I've seen that happen.
Yeah.
Now who were some of the outstanding bands for playing funerals? Who would you name?
Well, I would consider it now. What do you mean, now or?
In the old days.
Back when you said you were sometimes playing one every day.
Well, I was going to tell you, there was the Excelsior, I had one, the Torsita, two, Torsita, and then there was two. Just a second.
You were telling me about the outstanding bands of years ago for planned funerals.

You know, well, the best bands in life. It was the Excelsior, Arnold Brass Band, Torsita, original Torsita. I don't mean John and them young Torsita. I mean the original Torsita. Then there was the Ux Sand. And of course, Alan, he had a band of old and out there. He was pretty good, but highly average. He didn't have no way of, he said, the men managed to play with him. The way he'd do, if he'd get a job, he'd come and get me. If I'm a good man, if he's a good man, get him, I'd play him good. And other fellows didn't play so well. Didn't get no money on it. So, that's what I was playing. But I remember the Torsita, Arnold, and Sucks.
Well, about how far back did those bands go? Were they already playing when you came to New Orleans?

Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. They were playing. When I came here, because when I came here, I didn't get in no band for a good while. I went away for a while. I didn't know nobody. You understand what you mean?
Well, how long did it take you to get with a band? Came here in 1913.
After they found us, you understand what kind of man I was, I couldn't, the rest, I couldn't. They didn't think they'd come and knock them to do.
Well, what about, before the Big Storm, were you playing with bands?
Before the Big Storm, were you playing with bands?
Yeah, the Big Storm here. Well, yeah, yeah, yeah. You were playing with bands?
Yes. See, the Big Storm was in September of 1950.
Sure, sure. And you came here in 1913. Good man. So it wasn't too long. Well, you know. I guess it just seemed long when you were new in the city and things like that.
Well, but I'm going to tell you, you see, when I first came here, some of the guys wouldn't hire me because he would say I couldn't play home, switch home by head.

You understand? Well, of course, which I couldn't, you understand, but because of me, I always developed the region, you understand? And so, and then after that, they found out that I could do both of them, you see. So, I got in the Exelter, and they hired me on my good night, you know, on my good night. And, uh, I was a regular man, first time one day. I stayed there until they broke that.
Well, what kind of music did you used to play before you came to New Orleans? This may be going over something you talked to him about before, but I'd like to know.
What kind of music? What you mean, uh, horn? What kind of horn did you play?
No, I mean, what type of music? Were people playing the same jazz type of music other places?

The same kind of music. Sheet music. You know what I mean? But, uh, which was then, uh, the gym, I don't think. I remember it. He used to come down there and teach the band. The place is a granddaddy.
Now, out there in the country, did that band play funerals and parades?
Yeah, the band could play anything any other band. And that's why when I came there, I know it, much easier, it's under no noise. Because I learned in the country.
So you'd sort of just grown up playing, huh? That's right, yeah.
Did they have dirges out in the country? Yeah. Would they have funerals with a band of music?
Well, they'd have funerals, sometimes. But it wasn't often like this, you understand me, because they didn't get many people down that way.
Then you had more musicians down there than you had up here in proportion of the population. They died every season.
We had, uh, in our band, we had 16.
And that was a small place, wasn't it?
Yeah, yeah. It was a plantation, or 10.

How many people on the plantation would you say about? About two, three hundred. That's quite a large portion of them playing music, to add that up. So, uh, would the funerals down there be a little like the funerals up here, or a little bit different, or a lot different of them?

Well, you see, they didn't have the road to go down there that they have here, you see? But they died every day, and if they leave the church, they may go back to the cemetery, and come right on back. They couldn't make no wrong, but they had to make a decision.
Would they be supported by an organization down there, society?
Yes, we had a society called The Morning Light.
The Morning Light, huh? That's right. Were there any other societies?
No, no, no, no. Plantation, you see. This one had one society, you know, one light. Well, then you really didn't find moving to the city too different from living in the
country, did you?
Well, yeah, it wasn't much for anything.
I mean, because a lot of the things, I guess, the same customs are on the... Yes. Would they stay longer in church in the country than in the city, or would they stay about
the same length of time?

No, no, no. Well, you see, they would preach as a nurse, you see. They would wait to be as a nurse, and preach as a nurse, and then after they would come to the church, and in the daytime, it was about 12 o'clock, and about 2 o'clock you leave. You leave us, I see. And buried the body, and come on back. Well, was the church on the plantation? Absolutely. And was there just one church for everybody on the plantation, or were there different... Baptist Church. So everybody that was on the plantation was on the plantation. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. So that would be different. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right. Now what about the different churches here in the city?

Like, Methodists and Baptists and Baptists and Baptists and all those other churches, and they were just one church for everybody on the plantation, or were there different churches? Well, was the church on the plantation? Absolutely. And was there just one church for everybody on the plantation, or were there different...
Yes, they had one church in the city. You called the Massage in the Baptist Church.
So everybody that was on the plantation were Baptist. That's right. So that would be different. Yeah, that's right.
Now what about the different churches here in the city, like Methodists and Baptists and Catholics? How long would the funerals last for them?

Well, they see nothing at all. In other words, they're Catholics, and they wouldn't... They see, they used no band now, they didn't. But by the time back, we used to play for them, but they don't use no band at all. They're not Catholic.
About when was that rule came out about the Catholics?
Well, I couldn't exactly say, but it hasn't been too long. It's been a little while ago.
Before the Depression, or after? After the Depression. After 1929.
Because I see the time, I used to go to the church there on the Tudin Avenue. Yeah, the church there.
I know the one, you mean, out around Galvez?
No, around the... Across from the charity?
Yeah. St. Catherine?
Yeah, St. Catherine.
You buried people from that church? I buried people from that church.
Many times.
Was that before World War II? Yeah.
Yeah, I believe it was before. It's been a pretty good while. Because I remember the George, this place, the George McCunty. Yeah. The trumpet player.
What band was that? The Tuxedo. Well, you could check on that through the church records.
I was thinking, yeah. I would show you that. And the church records are showing that. Was it cut out?
Well, is there much difference between the Methodists and the Baptists?
Oh, I don't think it is. Excuse me.
Not that you've noticed. No, no, no.
Which lasts the longest? The Baptist or the Methodists?
Mm-hmm. I think I couldn't say. Which lasts the longest? Well, I guess the one who lived the longest. No, but I mean the preachers.
The preaching. Which preachers longest? Oh. I guess the Baptists.
They preach the longest. Yeah. But... That's been my experience.
The Methodists are much shorter than the Baptist.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, for the few things. Yeah, they're much shorter. Yeah.
Do you all ever play at any Episcopal funerals? Have they ever had a band of music? No.
No.
No other churches but Baptist and Methodist now? Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. What about the sanctified churches? Yeah.
I haven't been around in a long time. But sometimes the sanctified churches would have a band, no?
Well, I'm afraid of the sanctified. I don't remember.

I can't put it in my own. Maybe I have it and didn't notice. I don't ever remember it. No, is that what I'm saying? No. That's what I'm saying? No. No. No. No. No. No. I don't remember it. No, is that what I'm saying? No, I don't remember.
I don't remember. I don't remember.
Okay now, we're talking about the different denominations. What about the Catholic funerals? What were they like?

Well, I'm going to tell you, with them Catholic funerals, we used to play them after we leave the church, you see, and go, it's a distance, we would turn them loose, you see. And then they'd go in with the business.
How'd you turn them all loose?

Well, we'd go through the distance, so we'd get to the corner there and stand and divide ourselves, open up, you understand, and play what the funerals would be going through, you see. And then after they'd gone through, well, we'd come on back to the hall.
Well, was that because the cemetery was so far away from the territory?
Yes, yes. Sometimes the cemetery was so far away, that's right.
And so then after you turned them loose, you'd go into whatever kind of music you wanted to play, just like you were coming back from the cemetery? Absolutely right.
The right job.
Well, do they still sometimes turn them loose, for instance, if they're bearing them out in Gentilius? Yes, yes.
That's right.
And then the lake for the host, if you've got a feeling, they go ahead there, excuse me.

Yes, yes. Well, they were going to sit at this and then they stop. They open up and stand there and they play a piece of what they're going through and then that's going to all of them. Turn around and come on back.
Were they playing a dirge while they're going through or him or what?

Yes, yes. We'd play him or anything. We'd play him or anything. We'd play him or anything. We'd play him or anything. We'd play him. We'd play him. We'll dodge anyways and it'll be okay. Well, do the relatives of the person who's dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear ever ask you to play certain things or I mean? Well, yes. Sometimes they request for some piece to be played. They replace that for them. But mostly people just like the
old Steiners like just a closer walk with me. Yes, that's the idea. I could listen to that about a thousand times I think and it always sounds different. It always sounds beautiful. Yes,
and then I'll tell you one thing, the upper garden, that's a wonderful thing.
The upper garden. I don't know that I know that. Is it that words? Yes, you know that I have words. Well, I probably recognize it if I heard it, you know, but just don't know the name.

Well, if you ever have a feeling in the denny, if you ever go to the cemetery, just ask the place, uh, five or so, or the place, uh, five or so, or some of them, you prepare, uh, upper garden for you.
I love it myself. I love the place. Well, now, upper garden, do you play that by head with the Eureka?

No, no, no, no, no, no. They had that. They got that. Who wrote it out for you? It was Dumaine. He written all the things out. It's a little piece of piece, but that's why the manuscript was here. Uh-huh. Yeah. Well, now, where did Dumaine get him from? The book.

Would that be a hymn book or? Yes. It would be a hymn book he got out from, huh? That's what I see the book. Whee! And so, what would he have in the hymn book? He would have words? Words, new books. And what kind of music would go with it?

He would put that, you see, the way it is now, the hymn books, they have words and the music there, you see? Now, all he had to do is to transport the music, you understand? And put it in what key it is. And he ain't the best key for the band, you see? Well, and that's one thing he could do.
But they wouldn't have all the parts in the hymn book is what I'm getting at, huh?
Well, him, he would make parts for the band, for the bass part and everything else.
He would just arrange it then from the piano part?
He would arrange it then, absolutely. Absolutely. He would take that piano part there and arrange for everybody.

He would take that piano part. They played Wonderful Friday. Remember when they played Wonderful? I think that was, oh, right after we came out of church, maybe. They played Wonderful. That's one of his. Yeah, yeah, that's what they said. That's a beautiful one, too.

He was good. He's dead and gone, but he's missing. Did they have anybody else could arrange hymns like that? Well, I would say, no, no, he's as good as them. Some of them arranged, but they didn't, they couldn't get to the weed, you see? They had to, I want to recall, he must wait. He was good, but he didn't stay alone. He left me with me.

Yeah. I think he's in California now. Yeah. Bill Russell's on it. Yeah. He's around San Francisco. He still plays with the brass band. Yeah, he's an all-round man. Yeah. He is. Well, what did he arrange? Or what did he arrange? Well, he didn't, he didn't, he didn't, he didn't arrange anything.
Oh, I thought maybe he was an arranger like Dumaine. No, he wasn't. He knew it. a whole lot, you know.
You must really have to know your music
to be able to do something like that. To be able to show.
You see, I've got a list of questions. We might as well get down to that. Let's see. Now, how did you learn how to walk with a brass band? Did you learn that in the country or the city?

Well, I'll tell you, I came here, I had to learn over again. Because in the country, we walked, you see, just a tempo, we reached in the country, we had just a little bit faster. But then after I came here, I learned how to walk. I learned how to walk all over again.
Did they play burges a little faster out there?
Yes.
And they played the regular march tempo the same or fast?
The march tempo was small.

The march tempo was small, but the burges were low. Yeah. That's how I see it. Did you ever hear any outstanding preachers for funerals? Any men who really were supposed to be good? Any men who really were supposed to be good?
Yes. What do you mean in the country? Either in the country or here?
Yeah. Outstanding preachers in the country.
I told them by the name of Jim Jones, he was an outstanding preacher.
Well, what makes a preacher outstanding with him, and what does he do?

Well, I'm going to tell you, if he's outstanding, he can stand upon his own. You can get anywhere you can stand and do, you can get this for work and any other man do all the more. He just gets through with the people more.
That's that side. What are they, outstanding preachers talk loud or soft or what?
They're very soft.
Some of them. They're getting their head turned, I guess, like me sometimes. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
Ever hear of sunshine money? I would.

How many times have I heard it? I really want these. These two are too sassy for me. They jump up and tell them women what they got to do, bring them money, and they don't care where they get it from.
Mm-hm .
That doesn't sound like a preacher. That sounds like something else .
Yeah . That doesn't want to . How did he get much for him . Mm-hm .
I wanted to ask you about not only the outstanding bands for funerals, but some of the outstanding individual musicians in the band, you know.
Why did you think of that? That's a question, maybe.
Oh, I know. But I mean, say for example, could you name me a good baritone player and sort of describe what he did?
Well, there's not many baritone players now. No, they haven't got it.
And then times back, who would be some of the men for really playing?

Oh, they had a few men. They had a few men called Vic Gaspar. He was good because he was a trumpet player and a baritone player. And the first guy was George the Hooker. He was pretty good. He was a little old man. He got Alexander. Daddy. He was very good. On the baritone? Yeah. That's Adolf Alexander Sr. Yeah.
Yeah. Well, his daddy was. Yeah. Well, he's junior.
Tatch is junior. Yeah, that's right. Tatch is junior.
That's right.
He used to be good too, Tatch. You know, the Dumpier Band. There's a boy that pick up there, the baritone man. He'd pick up a drum one part and play any part of that.
He's a good musician.
You'd like to sing. Well, how would a man do like that on the baritone? What would you like to sing? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Vibrato you know, shaking or what he...
No, that's what I couldn't tell you. You couldn't tell me about the baritone. No, no, but because him you use...
They use their fingers a little different from the trombone.
Oh, oh, oh, oh, but you know the trombone and the baritone, they use the same finger.
Yeah, but I wondered if any of those guys you know would use the... shake their fingers to get an effect, you know, a little bit.
Oh, oh, oh, what do you mean by the... on the trombone? That's true, yeah?
No, no, I mean, you know how some guys, they'll be playing trumpet and they'll shake their fingers a little bit?
Yeah, yeah.
Just to give it a little vibrato, it gives it that little...
Sure, that's easy.
You do that on a baritone? Did you ever do that?
Sure, sure you do it.
Sure, sure. Who would have the most beautiful tone of those guys?
Oh, let's see, a fish.
They really had a beautiful tone? Yes, we don't think. What special numbers featured a baritone?
Well, I don't know. I couldn't say because... I didn't care what you put there, you know, he was so sweet and tasty.
Well, the number that gets me is that Westlund, you know, that's a beautiful part.

But, oh, no, let me tell you. The Westlund, it's even but one man ever played that thing on a baritone like he should be played. Because we was the first one in the good time, in the goddamn restaurant. Celestine, the first one, got that restaurant. A fella called John, quote it, and he's Dick. Dick, of course, you talk about God, that man, when he first got this piece, that man made everyone cry around the church. You see, the way he played that Westlund, he had such an expression in the tone, and he'd hold him most to the evangelist. And he'd get off it short and smooth. I was playing, I had to stop myself. He taught you how. Anybody in the whole church come in there. He had to have anything. He had to have anything. He had to have anything. And then the district service we had on base, he had to have anything. Oh, that long, tall, dark guy. And he, we had a man, that took his man. I'm telling you, we didn't care for nobody. He had to have nobody. He could take care of himself.
When you were saying that he had everybody in the church crying, did he play it inside the church?

No, coming up, you see, when they come back, when the boy was telling me to tell us to play. And then he started on this thing, he said, you mean John, John, John, for it? Yeah, go in, go in, go in, go in. Go to that bathroom, sir. And that man, he didn't want to cry. And I was like, I didn't know John. And then that was back, back on Clara. Clara, near, can't do it. Yeah, you know, so my back, they had the church so my back. But now, if things messes back down, if I go back down, I wouldn't know myself. But at them times, you know. But there's nobody to play the leg into it. And then again, the bathroom have a different effect too, you understand? Of course, or, the place is nice. But the real bathroom, all this.
Better than a tenor saxophone. Yeah, sure. Sure. Did they have any outstanding alto, those horn men?
Well, what I'm going to tell you, they had one, so far down, I think he put in the business now. One man, Barbara, he was good. Those fellows playing alto horn, mellophone.
Well, those fellows playing alto horn, mellophone, would they carry a melody like the baritone would sometimes?

No, no, no, no, what they do is they always have to be, sometimes, I'm sure what it comes through, but most of the time, you know, it's a big, big, big, big, big, big, big, big, big, big business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business business
Did they have anybody who was outstanding for trumpet solos?

Yeah. George McCulloch. That's one of the guys that nobody did 90 years ago. They used to fit him all the time. Any hot thing coming, the King Madras and things. They didn't come back. The boy gets back. He's been a little bit further. He's been trouble with that.
Would he specialize in funeral directors?
Anything. Anything. Concerts. Anything. We speak all of them.
Like Pajo today. Now that's what Pajo liked to do best is play a solo on the 3rd it seems
to me. Yeah, sure.
Because he'd rather play a funeral than eat a turkey dinner.

Well, me too. I would see my man when I was there. I'd be so glad I'd jump with that. I'd be the first and the first and the first job. I used to love it and I loved it up until long but I know I can't pay more for him. Because if a fellow can do a job and do it good, he makes it. That's between me. I know. I know. I didn't need nobody to tell them. But when I was there, I was going to go to the other. And then when they get up there, I'd be the first man out of it too. I'd get my first person every trip. Even though we know it.
Any other men that specialize in hims and durians other than McCollum?
Well, I think he was doing that. And he was the best around him. And at that time, he did. I think he was the best. And then Mr. Ithlap, he used to be pretty good too. Lionel Faber.
I'm trying to think about the different guys I've heard about his being good at Fennells. Alvin Alcorn played beautiful with Ole Manol and some. And Manuel Parage is supposed to have been good.

Oh, yeah. He was good. He was strong and everything. But you see, this boy, McCollum, he didn't blast nothing. But the tune came out and he said, he just as clear as anything. He didn't blast nothing. Of course, as a matter of fact, he was a strong man on the track. He didn't blast. But the other boy, McCollum, he didn't blast. I swore it to him. But you could hear it anyway. I see.
Let's see. Any outstanding clarinet players? Or... Anybody who would make you cry, you know what I'm saying.
No, excuse me, but I'll tell you, Lorenzo Teo. He was a really outstanding class player.
What would he do at a funeral that would be a special?

Oh, that's all I had? Yeah. Well, he was a good man. You want to get on the job then? He was white. And you could hear him. He didn't like it for you. They got nothing. You can't hear him. Them families, they said, supposed to be above everything in the band. You couldn't hear him anyway. But somebody got on the piano, you can't hear him. From here to the door there. I wouldn't have him. Left him. Yeah. And then they'd do it.
Well, why do you think that there aren't as many good musicians as they used to be?

Well, they had. Some of them, but you see, they just died there. And then again, these young, younger fellows come on now. They don't take up. They let the old fellows come back, you understand? I guess they haven't got as many, you understand? Because they all want them. Sacriform, sacriform. That's all they want. Sacriform.
Well, it's hard to have young E-flat clarinet players that I know around. Huh?
I can't think of any really young E-flat clarinet players. No, they just died there. That's what I wanted to do. They're not one around. No, they're the only one that satriform.
Well, is that why they seem to not bury people with a band of music as often as they used to? Or why?

Oh, no, no. No, it isn't that. No, they don't bury. It's used to it. The money that you were growing now. I guess the big fish, they eat up there. The little fish when they got the money. That's very great.
People don't have as much money now for $15.
But they make money now. They don't have as much money. They got money, but they're not too big fish. Eat up the little fish. That's where you go.
Well, about how often would you say that these days, you said that they used to have maybe one funeral every day. But about how often do they have funerals with music now?

Well, they can't tell. Sometimes you may have a feeling. Two or three weeks straight. And then you get in that, that it would go off. But you see, the times back, they used to have more society. You used to play with, you know, by a band. And clubs, you used to play with a band. But now they haven't got many clubs. You see, that makes the job going on. They don't have as many. As many people dying, they did die. But you don't have as many people dying who went to the club. Mm-hmm. That's right.
Well, you just said something about societies and something about clubs. Are societies and clubs different?
Yes, society and clubs different.
Well, what's the difference?
Well, what you see, with the club, it's more for pleasure, you see. Mm-hmm. And society is more for you, you know, being sick, you see.
Well, the club would be like the Zillers then or something like that.
Yeah, like them, they see that they're pleasure. Mm-hmm. And they're buried though with the music though. Yeah.
Well, what else do they have besides societies and clubs? Is there anything else like that?
No, I don't think anything is different than any side of clubs.
Mm-hmm. Well, what would you call a young man's Olympian Benevolent Protective Association?
That's a society.

That's a society. The Jolly Bunch? That's a club. I think I see already what you're talking about. I can tell this from the name. Yeah. The Jolly Dab. I tell you right away. When they have that benevolent of protection, you know what it is. That's got to be a society. Absolutely.
They're all in the corporate.

If they say Social and Pleasure Club, you know what they say. Yeah, I would say. Mm-hmm. You're right. You could go back to some of those different men on the different instruments that were outstanding in the street. Like, you mentioned one bass player. What about some of the others? What was that?

Well, Eddie Cason was outstanding. And so another person called Joe Howard. He was really outstanding man. Because he used to play trumpet. And then that guy, he would go on the bass. But what he had in the other person, too, you call Pierre Anderson. And then he said, I tried it on the bass. And the first time I tried it on his trumpet. And then the bass, when he got the bass, the instrument played bass. And if he did bass, he ran off with it. You see, any man that a trumpet, if he ever could play the trumpet first, and then if he came up to a bass, man, he didn't run for that bass. Because the bass is so slow on the bass, because sometimes you catch some passes, it's fast. But you see, if a fella used to play a trumpet, you know, instead of that, he just was going over you. That's the way each other came. Joe Howard was one of them. And so he said a fella was just on there. And they called Pierre after a Hadsden cousin. Hadsden bond. He was really good.
Oh, while we're at it, what about this fella, Munster for Johnson, you were telling me about?

Yes, he's such a young man. He came to the Charlie Hospital one day, and I think you just had him there when I was in the Charlie Hospital. Yeah, because on this bed number two, his cousin was in this bed number two.
Did they call him Moe's too?
Yeah, they did call him Moe's, but his name is Mustaford Johnson. But the sentence was called Doe, which they called him what kind of name, but his red name is Mustaford Johnson.
Well, we'll have to go back and look for him. He lived up in the old asylum.
He lived up there somewhere. I don't know why he lived there. I'm going to tell the truth.

Well, we'll find him. I think he lives near a lemon. I'll get lemon to get him in contact with me. Yeah, he's going to throw that. If I can find lemon. That's another problem. Lemon doesn't have a telephone either.
He's a big guy.
Now, let's see. We've been over most of the instruments except the drums and the trombone. Who were some of the drummers that were good at that band?
What do you mean? The bass drum?
Bass drum and snare.
Well, I don't know. I understand. He was one of the outstanding. What band was this? The Tursedo? The Cilestine Tursedo. I mean the old rhythm Tursedo. I mean the Tursedo was there now.
And what instruments did he play? Bass drum.
He used to play a trap. I mean, he'd play string band too, but... In that brass band, he was right there with you. All the time.
And what made him good? What did he have?
I don't know. I don't know what happened, but I know he had a feeling for music. That's what I could tell you.
Was he good especially on Durses or the bass drum and stuff?

Any one of them. Any one of them. They come on and they're dodging. I'm going to tell you the fact that we had the best band in town. The Tursedo. Because you can't find with the bass song. We had the best bass players. We had the best bass tune. We had the best bass tune. And you come on trombone. It was a little tough. And then, you know, both bands had a good drum. You see. And then, after, we had a problem for our band. And, uh, we planned it. Well, I don't tell you. Our band was no doubt that the Tursedo band, the Pauvich, of course, I don't tell you. But, you know, the other band, they let you go. You know, don't you think that you could go to sleep now, huh? And the other bands, you had to wait. You had to wait.
Would they have more than one band at a funeral level? Oh, man.

I've seen time after some of them died. But, they had about four or five bands. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Yeah, you know, yeah.
Well, cut it off for a second.
How many bands they have? They must have had about four or five bands. I tell you, if you really want to find out, if you see Peter Booker, he can tell more about me.

segments.title: Opening: recording location and date
segments.summary: Interviewer states where and when the tape is being recorded, then resumes the church collection topic.

segments.title: Church collections, envelopes and dollar matches
segments.summary: Henry explains how offerings are collected by basket, envelope and walking around the table, and what a dollar match is. Money goes to the church, not the preacher.

segments.title: How societies choose brass bands
segments.summary: Bands do not give samples; society members know every band. Henry points to people who keep the society records.

segments.title: Church funeral service, viewing the body and dress
segments.summary: Order of a funeral service: viewing the body, half lid, flowers, how the body is dressed, and whether Masons hire bands.

segments.title: From church to cemetery and back to the hall
segments.summary: What happens at the cemetery, the route back to the society hall, and the music played returning. Musicians feed themselves.

segments.title: Drum rolls, return tunes and march tempo
segments.summary: How drum rolls and bass drum beats signal the band, what tunes are played on return, and tempo.

segments.title: Pay for funerals and how it was spent
segments.summary: Funeral pay is five to seven dollars with the leader getting more; it was two dollars when he arrived. He spent much on drink and also played nightly dances.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and coming to New Orleans
segments.title: Outstanding old funeral bands
segments.summary: Henry names the Excelsior, Arnold brass band, the original Tuxedo, and a band led by Alan as the best funeral bands.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and coming to New Orleans
segments.title: Arriving in New Orleans in 1913 and joining the Excelsior
segments.summary: Arriving in 1913, he had trouble getting hired because he could not read or play by head, then joined the Excelsior as a regular.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and coming to New Orleans
segments.title: Country band and funerals on the plantation
segments.summary: Before New Orleans he played sheet music in a country plantation band of sixteen, with funerals and a society called Morning Light.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and coming to New Orleans
segments.title: Church on the plantation versus the city
segments.summary: Plantation funerals ran midday with one Baptist church for everyone, contrasted with city churches.

segments.title: Catholic funerals and bands, St. Catherine church
segments.summary: Catholic churches stopped using bands; Henry recalls burying people from St. Catherine and George McCullum with the Tuxedo.

segments.title: Baptist and Methodist services and which churches use bands
segments.summary: Baptist preaching lasts longer than Methodist; Episcopal and sanctified churches have no bands.

segments.title: Turning the band loose at distant funerals
segments.summary: With far cemeteries, bands play through the procession, split and play for the funeral passing, then return to the hall.

segments.title: Hymn arrangements: Closer Walk and Dumaine
segments.summary: Henry praises Dumaine, who arranged hymns for the band from hymn-book piano parts, and discusses other arrangers.

segments.title: Learning to walk with a brass band in the city
segments.summary: He had to learn marching again in New Orleans because the country tempo was faster.

segments.title: Outstanding preachers
segments.summary: Henry names Jim Jones as an outstanding country preacher and comments on preachers and money.

segments.title: Outstanding baritone players
segments.summary: Names of good baritone players, including Vic Gaspar, Alexander and Tatch, and discussion of vibrato and fingering.

segments.title: The hymn Westlawn played on baritone
segments.summary: Henry describes one baritone player whose playing of Westlawn made everyone cry.

segments.title: Alto horn and mellophone players
segments.summary: Brief discussion of alto horn and mellophone players and their role.

segments.title: Trumpet soloists: George McCullum
segments.summary: George McCullum was the outstanding trumpet soloist for hymns and dirges, a clean player who did not blast.

segments.title: Clarinet player Lorenzo Tio
segments.summary: Henry names Lorenzo Tio as an outstanding clarinet player, though hard to hear in the band.

segments.chapter: Decline of funeral bands and societies
segments.title: Why fewer musicians and funerals today
segments.summary: Henry says good musicians died, young players do not take it up, and fewer clubs and societies mean fewer funerals.

segments.chapter: Decline of funeral bands and societies
segments.title: Societies versus social clubs
segments.summary: Societies are for sickness and burial benefit, clubs for pleasure; examples of each are sorted out.

segments.title: Bass players and Mustaford Johnson
segments.summary: Names of outstanding bass players who began on trumpet, and a young musician called Moe, Mustaford Johnson.

segments.title: Tuxedo drummers and number of bands at funerals
segments.summary: Henry praises the Celestin Tuxedo drummer and says the Tuxedo was the best band; big funerals had four or five bands.
